newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Brussels film fest welcomes horror director Craven.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Brussels film fest welcomes horror director Craven.

text.p: American thriller director Wes Craven, whose latest film "Scream" was cut by U.S. censors objecting to evisceration and protracted slashing scenes, believes horror movies must show the reality of violent acts.

"Real violence as opposed to screen violence is sometimes very protracted and quite unpredictable," Craven told Reuters during the fifteenth Brussels International Festival of Fantasy, Thriller and Science Fiction Films this month.
"I think what censorship does is try to make you lie about the essence of violence. I hope that the essential truth is still there in the film, but I know part of it is missing."

Craven, who established himself in the thriller-horror genre with films such as "A Nightmare on Elm Street", says that rather than encouraging violence themselves his movies allow the audience to work through their own fears.
He compares this to a soldier training for combat without being hurt in the process.
"They are boot camps for the psyche. They take the fears in the audience, bring them into a story and deal with them in a way that exorcises those fears rather than causing new ones.

"When that works, the audience will come out relieved. That's why you see audiences coming out of a scary movie laughing and jumping up and down -- rather than coming out depressed or thinking 'Who can I kill now?'."
FILM FESTIVAL ATTRACTS YOUNG FANS

Gigi Etienne, one of the organisers of the Brussels fantasy film festival, said the average age of its horror enthusiasts was about 25 years old. "The late night sessions attract a younger public still," she added.
Over 50,000 people attended the two-week event which ended on March 22, seeing more than 60 films from Europe, North and South America, Australia, New Zealand and Japan, including 11 world premieres.
Exquisite body paintings, a vampires' midnight ball and presentations marking the 100 years since Bram Stoker published his Dracula tale were among the side attractions.
The Italian film "Luna e l'Altra" (Luna and the Other) by Maurizio Nichetti, a story set in the 1950s about the conflict between a woman and her shadow, won the festival's Grand Prize.
The prize for best European fantasy film went to Spain's "Tesis" (Thesis), directed by 23-year-old Alejandro Amenabar.
Craven's "Scream" was one of four European premieres.
It is a grisly, psychological thriller which has actresses Drew Barrymore and Neve Campbell playing two high school girls who are stalked by a sociopath in their small California town.
At the same time the film parodies the usual rules of horror movies, where characters who go to answer the door, hide in the closet or let out piercing screams are always doomed.
"Because it's basically subversive, 'Scream' shows that as soon as you learn the rule it no longer applies," Craven said.

"It also looks at the fact that horror films are a source of amusement for teenagers -- and at whether this makes them cynical or (people) just trying to deal with the craziness of the world, whether these films hurt or help them if they should encounter horror in their own lives."
CRAVEN GETS INSPIRATION FROM GREEK MYTHS
A script writer as well as a director, Craven said several of his previous films were inspired by newspaper stories.
"You can't write anything more bizarre than the things which are really going on in life. It's important to bring up this essential matter in a film rather than deny it's there."

Craven, 47, has signed a deal to write a novel, which he says looks at the frontiers of science and medicine, the artificial extension of life, and at how governments could use this to enhance their power.
A one-time humanities professor, Craven said his time teaching Greek mythology had also been a great source of inspiration.

"When I sit down and make a horror film I ask what Greek myth goes into this -- the descent into hell, or the monster that has to be approached deviously in order to win its power. I try to put those same timeless elements into the films that I make.

"Even though you are making the audience laugh and scream, you are talking about things that are ancient and very primal, and very important, and can sometimes not be treated in any other way except with stories like these."
